title: In trying to prop up the yen, the US wants to have its cake and eat it too
gist: On July 31, 2026 the US Treasury joined Japan in its first yen-buying intervention since June 1998, after Japan burned an estimated $87 billion of reserves over two days to arrest a mere 4.6 percent yen slide. Obstfeld argues the operation is incoherent: US tariffs and the $550 billion Japanese investment pledge structurally weaken the yen, a stronger yen contradicts Bessent's 'strong dollar' talk, and the real motive - sparing the fragile Treasury market from Japanese reserve liquidation, plus a request to 'upsize' the Fed's FIMA repo facility - pushes the US toward fiscal dominance.

insights.claim: The US Treasury joined Japanese authorities in a joint FX intervention to strengthen the yen on July 31, 2026, the first US intervention in support of the yen since June 1998.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: A 28-year precedent break signals Washington is now willing to use its balance sheet on FX; treat USD/JPY upside as carrying explicit official intervention risk rather than pure carry.
insights.quote: The US action was notable as its first intervention in support of the yen since June 1998
insights.locator: In a highly unusual move, the US Treasury

insights.claim: Japan spent an estimated $87 billion of its foreign exchange reserves buying yen over the last two days of July, while the US Treasury added only a relatively small amount of financial support but a substantial political signal.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The size ratio shows Japan bears the cost while the US supplies signaling; watch Japan's reserve drawdown pace as the true constraint on how long the defense can run.
insights.quote: Japan spent an estimated $87 billion(link is external) of its foreign exchange reserves to buy yen over the last two days of July.
insights.locator: But Japan spent an estimated $87 billion

insights.claim: The yen had depreciated only about 4.6 percent against the dollar since Japan's prior solo intervention in spring 2025 - not a massive or sudden move - meaning the intervention trigger was political rather than disorderly-market driven.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: A 4.6 percent move as an intervention trigger implies a far lower pain threshold than markets assumed, tightening the implied band on USD/JPY.
insights.quote: The yen had depreciated by around 4.6 percent against the dollar since the Japanese government's prior solo intervention last spring, hardly a massive or sudden move.
insights.locator: The yen had depreciated by around 4.6 percent

insights.claim: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent framed the yen intervention geopolitically rather than economically, saying the administration 'delivers for America's trusted partners.'
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: FX policy is being used as alliance currency, so intervention odds now track diplomatic relationships as much as valuation - relevant for KRW, TWD and other allied Asian crosses.
insights.quote: The Trump Administration delivers for America's trusted partners.
insights.locator: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent gave it a geopolitical gloss

themes.theme: Why intervention cannot work: the FX framework

insights.claim: Exchange rate trends depend primarily on monetary and fiscal policies plus long-run trade developments, making FX intervention at best a short-term corrective to disorderly moves rather than a way to change a currency's path.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Use intervention-driven yen strength as a fade opportunity unless BOJ tightening or US fiscal consolidation actually changes the rate differential.
insights.quote: exchange rate trends depend primarily on monetary and fiscal policies, as well as long-run trade developments, making foreign exchange interventions at best a short-term corrective to disorderly exchange rate movements
insights.locator: As the floating exchange rate system evolved

insights.claim: The Treasury's newly activist exchange rate stance rests on the illusion that inherent policy tradeoffs don't apply, which produces inconsistent policies likely to raise economic volatility.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Higher policy inconsistency argues for owning FX and rates volatility rather than carry; the regime raises the odds of abrupt reversals.
insights.quote: A more activist role toward exchange rates, which the US Treasury is now embracing, relies on the illusion that inherent policy tradeoffs don't apply. This misguided belief leads to inconsistent policies likely to raise economic volatility.
insights.locator: A more activist role toward exchange rates

insights.claim: The 1998 US-Japan intervention had a stronger systemic rationale - an Asian financial crisis and China holding the yuan stable - and was conditioned on Japanese promises of financial sector reform and demand stimulus, yet even that had little enduring impact on the yen.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The best-case historical comparator failed on the currency; expect the 2026 version, which lacks conditionality, to fail faster.
insights.quote: Even so, the intervention had little enduring impact on the yen, and Japan's efforts proved insufficient to turn its economy around before new shocks hit it.
insights.locator: Cakeism is bad policy

insights.claim: The 2026 intervention lacks the conditionality of 1998 - there is no paired commitment by Japan to address the underlying causes of yen depreciation - so it is a short-term response to policy dilemmas on both sides of the Pacific and will not work over the longer term.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Base case is renewed yen weakness after the intervention effect decays; the tell would be absence of Japanese fiscal or structural commitments alongside future operations.
insights.quote: Foreign exchange intervention is not a free lunch. It is not even a free cake.
insights.locator: In contrast, last month's US intervention

themes.theme: Tariffs versus the yen: the trade contradiction

insights.claim: US trade actions against Japan - multiple tariffs, most recently under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, plus investigations - are themselves a driver of yen weakness that intervention cannot mask.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Every new tariff escalation on Japan mechanically adds to the yen-weakening force the same government is fighting; track Section 301 actions as a leading indicator for USD/JPY.
insights.quote: Japan's yen intervention, supported by the US Treasury, cannot long mask the fact that the hostile American trade actions against Japan are one driver of a weaker yen.
insights.locator: Trade policy confusion

insights.claim: Japan's trade-deal commitment to invest $550 billion in US projects selected by the administration weakens the yen, because more Japanese investment into America requires a bigger Japanese trade surplus.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The $550bn pledge is a structural yen-negative capital outflow; the more of it that gets deployed, the harder intervention has to work against it.
insights.quote: Other things being equal, these factors would weaken the yen (Japanese exporters must find new buyers, while more investment into America requires a bigger Japanese trade surplus).
insights.locator: Under its so-called "trade deal" with the Trump administration

insights.claim: Bessent fears a weak yen could catalyze broader Asian currency weakness - and the same Asian countries are targets of US protectionist policies and threats, making the US the source of the pressure it wants to contain.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Watch for intervention or jawboning spreading to other Asian FX; the Treasury has signaled it views regional currency weakness as a policy problem.
insights.quote: Bessent has noted that currencies throughout Asia are weak and expressed fears(link is external) that a weak yen could catalyze broader currency weakness regionally.
insights.locator: Bessent has noted that currencies throughout Asia are weak

insights.claim: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's expansive fiscal plans, driven partly by higher defense spending the Trump administration favors, worry markets against an already massive Japanese debt-to-GDP ratio and now-positive nominal yen interest rates.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Fiscal expansion plus positive nominal rates is a JGB term-premium story; watch the long end of the JGB curve as the transmission channel into the yen.
insights.quote: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's expansive fiscal plans, driven in part by higher defense spending that the Trump administration favors, worry markets
insights.locator: To be sure, there are other fundamental sources of yen weakness

insights.claim: Japanese real interest rates remain far below US levels, which continues to fuel yen weakness regardless of intervention.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The real-rate gap is the core carry driver; yen recovery requires that gap to close, so trade the US-Japan real rate differential, not the intervention headlines.
insights.quote: Nonetheless, Japanese real interest rates remain far below US levels, giving additional fuel to yen weakness.
insights.locator: Nonetheless, Japanese real interest rates

insights.claim: Bessent has called on Japan to raise interest rates and BOJ officials are signaling they may well do so in September 2026, but Japanese authorities face a dilemma between hiking to strengthen the yen and dampen inflation versus worsening fiscal sustainability.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: A September BOJ hike is the single most tradable near-term catalyst flagged here; position for JGB yield and yen reaction, and note US pressure raises the odds.
insights.quote: Bank of Japan (BOJ) officials are signaling that they may well do so in September
insights.locator: Bessent has called(link is external) on Japan to raise interest rates

themes.theme: Strong dollar rhetoric versus weak dollar goal

insights.claim: Bessent's advocacy of a 'strong dollar' and promotion of the dollar's premier international role, including global dollar-based stablecoins, is contradicted by the intervention itself, whose stated goal is a more competitive - i.e. weaker - dollar.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Discount official strong-dollar rhetoric; the revealed preference is dollar depreciation, which argues for structurally short-dollar positioning against allied Asian currencies.
insights.quote: this detail doesn't alter the fact that the fundamental and, in fact, stated goal of the intervention is a more competitive (i.e., weaker) dollar
insights.locator: Strong dollar or weak dollar?

insights.claim: The Treasury sold euros rather than dollars for yen on July 31, likely to frame the operation as yen-strengthening rather than dollar-weakening.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The choice of funding currency is the tell for how future US interventions will be dressed up; euro crosses can be collateral damage in US-Japan FX operations.
insights.quote: One reason the Treasury sold euros rather than dollars for yen on July 31 may have been to signal a yen-strengthening rather than a dollar-weakening operation
insights.locator: Strong dollar or weak dollar?

insights.claim: The Treasury sold euros without consulting euro area authorities in advance, a small monetary gesture that conveyed a strong negative signal about US cooperation in managing the international financial commons - and markets have taken note.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Erosion of G7 FX coordination norms raises the tail risk of uncoordinated or competing interventions; a euro-positive reserve-diversification argument over time.
insights.quote: Treasury sold euros without consulting euro area authorities in advance, much to their annoyance
insights.locator: Note 1

themes.theme: Treasury market fragility, FIMA and fiscal dominance

insights.claim: A key motive for US participation was that the Treasury market has become increasingly fragile as US public debt has grown, and further large-scale Treasury sales by a holder as big as Japan could stress the market and raise borrowing rates; US yen buying lets Japan liquidate fewer Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The intervention is partly a rates-market defense - Japanese FX defense and US long-end yields are now linked, so watch Japanese reserve composition as a UST supply risk.
insights.quote: The Treasury market has become increasingly fragile(link is external) as the US public debt has grown. Further large-scale sales of Treasury securities by a holder as big as Japan could stress the market and raise borrowing rates.
insights.locator: What's more, one motive for the US yen intervention

insights.claim: The contradiction between America's ongoing fiscal deficit, which is gradually eroding the Treasury's funding advantage, and the dollar's reserve currency role cannot be resolved by asking foreign reserve holders to limit their use of dollars; the fix requires greater US fiscal prudence and Treasury market infrastructure upgrades.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Absent fiscal consolidation or market-structure reform, the US funding advantage keeps eroding - a structural argument for higher term premium and gold/non-dollar reserve assets.
insights.quote: The solution requires greater US fiscal prudence and upgrades to Treasury market infrastructure to facilitate trade even when large shocks occur.
insights.locator: The contradiction between America's ongoing fiscal deficit

insights.claim: Bessent 'encouraged' the Federal Reserve to 'upsize' the FIMA repo facility, which was designed for temporary emergency Treasury acquisitions to support market functioning - not to stabilize Treasury borrowing rates by accommodating foreign authorities' exchange rate operations absent financial stability threats.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Any Fed move to upsize or routinize FIMA is a concrete marker of institutional erosion; watch FOMC pushback as the signal on Fed independence.
insights.quote: It was not designed to stabilize Treasury borrowing rates by accommodating foreign authorities' exchange rate management operations, absent immediate financial stability threats.
insights.locator: Pressure on the Fed

insights.claim: Blurring the emergency-liquidity and FX-management roles of the FIMA facility would move the US monetary regime a step closer to fiscal dominance, at the expense of Fed credibility, and would likely be resisted by the FOMC.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Fiscal-dominance risk is the tail trade here: steepeners, breakeven inflation and gold benefit if the Fed's balance sheet becomes an adjunct to Treasury financial diplomacy.
insights.quote: Blurring the line between these two roles would move the US monetary regime a step closer to fiscal dominance.
insights.locator: Pressure on the Fed

insights.claim: It has not been disclosed whether the Federal Reserve put its own balance sheet behind the July 31 intervention alongside the Treasury's, unlike most past US foreign exchange interventions.
insights.speaker: Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Disclosure of Fed participation - or its absence - in the quarterly FX operations report is a direct read on how much independence the Fed is conceding.
insights.quote: Whether the Fed even put its own balance sheet behind the July 31 intervention along with the Treasury's, as has been the case in most past US foreign exchange interventions, has not been disclosed.
insights.locator: Pressure on the Fed
